Blog Title: Staying Sane in a World That Won't Cooperate
Blog Details: The world is not going to slow down or become more reasonable. The question is not how to fix it — it is how to stay whole inside it.
Blog Rich Title: Staying Sane in a World That Won't Cooperate
Blog Rich Text:
The goal was never a perfect life. It was always a grounded one.

I had a conversation recently with a professional who, by every visible measure, had things together. Good career. Stable family. Active faith. But she told me something that has stayed with me since.

She said, I spend most of my energy just trying not to lose it. Not building anything. Not growing anything. Just holding the line against everything coming at me.

She was not describing a crisis. She was describing a Tuesday.

Most people are quietly wrestling with exactly this. Not a dramatic breakdown but a steady, low-level exhaustion that comes from living responsibly in a world that constantly gives you reasons not to. Systems that fail. People who disappoint. Situations that have no clean resolution. Days that end with more undone than done and a vague sense that you are only just keeping up.

Nobody talks about this honestly enough. So let us.

Life Being Honest Is Not a Personal Crisis

The first thing worth saying is this. Things will annoy you. People will disappoint you. Systems will fail you. Plans will fall apart. And sometimes, no matter how hard you work or how well you prepare, there is simply no clean solution available. That is not a sign that you are doing life wrong. That is just life being honest with you.

A significant amount of the internal pressure people carry comes not from the difficulties themselves but from the gap between what they expected and what they got. The expectation that a responsible, faithful, hardworking person should somehow be exempt from the friction of ordinary life. They are not. Nobody is. And releasing that expectation is one of the quieter but more important acts of self-care available to anyone.

Stop Trying to Control What Was Never Yours to Control

A large portion of daily exhaustion is spent on things that were never within your control to begin with. Other people's decisions. Other people's moods. The pace at which institutions move. The way a conversation lands. Whether someone chooses to be fair.

The moment you stop trying to manage what was never yours to manage, you get yourself back. Not everything. But enough. Enough to think clearly, to respond rather than react, to bring something to the day rather than just surviving it.

This is not the same as giving up or becoming indifferent. You can care deeply about something and still accept that you cannot force its outcome. Influence what you can. Release what you cannot. The line between those two things is where a lot of peace lives.

Annoyance Is Information, Not Instruction

Noticing that something is wrong, frustrating, or unjust is fine. It is even necessary. Annoyance has a function. It tells you that something matters to you, that a boundary has been crossed, that something needs attention.

But there is a significant difference between annoyance as a signal and annoyance as a driver. When you let what irritates you determine your mood, your words, your decisions, and your energy for the rest of the day, you have allowed information to become instruction. And that is a costly transfer of power.

Notice the thing. Decide what, if anything, it requires of you. Then move. Do not set up residence in it.

Not Everything Deserves Your Peace

Some things you tolerate. Some things you address. Some things you walk away from. Knowing which is which is not weakness. It is one of the most practical forms of wisdom available to a person trying to stay well in a difficult world.

The person who treats every irritation as a battle to be won ends up exhausted and isolated. The person who tolerates everything ends up hollowed out and quietly resentful. The wise path is a discerning one. Pick what is worth your energy. Guard what cannot be replaced. Let the rest go without guilt.

Your peace is not an automatic right. It is something you actively protect. And protecting it sometimes means making decisions that other people do not understand or agree with. That is acceptable.

Find Your Anchors and Guard Them

Every person who stays well in a difficult world has something that keeps them grounded. Routines that bring order to the day. People who tell them the truth. A faith that holds when circumstances do not. Values that do not shift depending on who is in the room.

Whatever genuinely anchors you, guard it. Not casually. Deliberately. Because the world will not remind you to tend to it. In fact the world will reliably and consistently offer you a hundred reasons to neglect it. The noise will always be louder than the anchor unless you make a deliberate choice about which one gets your attention first.

One of the things I have observed consistently in the people I coach through LTE is that those who are holding up well are not the ones with the least problems. They are the ones with the clearest anchors. They know what grounds them. They return to it regularly. And that consistency, unglamorous as it is, is what keeps them from drifting.

Give Yourself Permission to Not Have All the Answers

There is a particular kind of pressure that comes from believing you should always know what to do next. That uncertainty is a problem to be solved rather than a season to be navigated. That not having a clear path forward is a failure of some kind.

It is not. Some seasons are genuinely unclear. Some questions do not have clean answers yet. Some situations require you to sit with the discomfort of not knowing before the way forward becomes visible. That is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is a sign that you are in the middle of something real.

Staying responsible does not always mean having a plan. Sometimes it simply means staying decent, staying present, and refusing to become someone you would not recognise. That is enough. On some days, it is everything.

A Grounded Life Is Built, Not Found

This is one of the conversations that sits at the heart of . Not because staying sane is a small thing but because it is the foundation everything else is built on. You cannot build a purposeful life, a meaningful career, a strong marriage, or a clear sense of direction from a place of quiet fragmentation and constant reactivity.

LTE was built for the person who is holding it together on the outside but knows something is unsettled underneath. The person who is capable and driven but running on the wrong fuel. The person who needs not more motivation but more grounding. More clarity about who they are, what anchors them, and what they are actually building.

The world will not cooperate. It never has and it never will. But a person who knows what grounds them, who has done the honest work of getting clear on their anchors, their values, and their direction, that person does not need the world to cooperate. They are already standing on something the world cannot move.

The goal was never a perfect life.

It was always a grounded one.

Blog Title: The Final Word
Blog Details: A closing reflection on everything this series has tried to say, and the one thing it has been saying all along.
Blog Rich Title: The Final Word
Blog Rich Text:
Wisdom Is Not a Mantra.

A closing reflection on everything this series has tried to say, and the one thing it has been saying all along.

We live in the age of the mantra.

Short, confident, repeatable phrases that promise to simplify the complexity of human life into something you can carry in your pocket. Be present. Choose joy. Speak your truth. Work hard and be kind. Do it scared. You only live once. See it. Say it. Sorted.

There is nothing wrong with a good mantra. At its best, a mantra is a compressed reminder of a principle worth returning to. A handle on something true. The problem is not the mantra. The problem is what happens when the mantra replaces the thinking rather than prompting it. When the phrase becomes the destination rather than the doorway. When we stop at the slogan and never enter the room it was pointing toward.

Wisdom cannot be compressed into a mantra. It was never designed to be. It is too alive, too contextual, too deeply dependent on the character of the person carrying it to survive that kind of reduction. A mantra can be memorised in a moment. Wisdom takes a lifetime. And the difference between those two timescales is not incidental. It is the entire point.

What This Series Has Been Saying

This series began with a simple question. What is wisdom? And it has taken several parts to begin to answer it honestly, because wisdom is the kind of subject that resists the quick summary. Every time you think you have it contained, it opens into something larger.

Part One established the foundation. Wisdom is not intelligence, not age, not knowledge, not cleverness, not caution, and not spirituality alone. It is the capacity to see clearly, judge rightly, and act appropriately across the full complexity of real life. Scripture places its beginning in the fear of the Lord, its availability in the generosity of God, its character in the fruit it produces, and its fullest expression in the person of Christ himself.

Part Two took wisdom into the room where it is most publicly tested: leadership and followership. Wise leaders understand that their role is responsibility carried, not authority exercised. Wise followers maintain their own interior life while serving wholeheartedly. And both sides of the room share the same foundation: genuine self-knowledge, a moral anchor above the relationship, and the courage to be honest when honesty costs something.

Part Three brought wisdom into the most intimate arena of all: marriage. The piece that perhaps carries the most personal weight in this series. Love brought you to the altar. Wisdom is what carries you through everything that comes after. Knowing the difference between a person and a pattern. Knowing when to speak and when to hold the silence. Understanding forgiveness not as a performance but as a genuine release. Recognising that being right is not the point when the health of the whole is at stake.

Part Four addressed conflict. Not as a problem to be avoided but as a reality to be navigated wisely. Conflict is not your enemy. Unexamined conflict is. The series argued that wisdom in conflict goes two levels deep, addressing what happened and what it meant. That timing matters as much as truth. That peacemaking and peacekeeping are not the same thing. And that the goal of conflict wisdom is never simply to end the argument, but to use the conflict as an opportunity to build something stronger than what existed before it.

Part Five turned to communication, the medium through which wisdom or its absence becomes most visible. Words carry the weight of death and life. Tone carries more than words. The unspoken communicates what speech sometimes cannot. Wise communication is oriented outward rather than inward, toward the person rather than the performance. And the standard Ephesians 4:15 gives, speaking the truth in love, is the hardest thing in communication to consistently maintain precisely because it refuses to allow truth and love to operate separately.

And between Part Five and this closing piece, the series paused on a distinction that may be the most theologically significant observation in the entire collection: the difference between the awareness of truth and the knowledge of truth. That truth received intellectually and truth integrated experientially are not the same thing. That the pain of the first time you choose the truth over the instinct is not a sign that you have failed. It is the mechanism by which truth moves from your head into your bones. The exam that keeps returning is not punishment. It is invitation. And you have not truly known a truth until the situation that tests it no longer costs you what it once did.

And Then There Is the Mantra

See it. Say it. Sorted.

It has become, in many communities and conversations, a shorthand for a certain kind of bold, unfiltered, direct engagement with life. Name what you see. Say what you mean. Move forward. There is something in it that sounds like wisdom. And in the right hands, at the right moment, with the right preparation, it can be.

But after everything this series has covered, the mantra deserves a more honest examination.

Did you actually see it? Or did you see it through the filter of a wound that was activated before the situation even began? Proverbs 18:17 reminds us that the first account of anything sounds convincing, including the account we give ourselves. Wisdom checks the lens before it trusts what the lens is showing.

Should you actually say it? Not every true thing needs to be spoken. Not every accurate observation needs to be shared at the moment it forms. The question wisdom requires before speaking is not simply did I see it, but does saying it build up, does it fit this occasion, does it give grace to the person receiving it. Ephesians 4:29 holds that standard without apology. And a significant amount of what people call honest communication fails all three tests simultaneously.

And is it sorted? Sorted implies completion. Resolution. The clean closing of an account. But anyone who has lived in real relationship knows that saying something and sorting something are frequently separated by a considerable distance. Sorted requires that the other person has genuinely received what was said. It requires that both parties have moved toward understanding. It requires patience, follow-through, and the humility to recognise that the conversation you thought would resolve something has sometimes only opened a wound that now needs careful, unhurried tending.

The mantra is not wrong. Avoidance is a real problem. Silence that masquerades as wisdom is a real problem. The person who sees clearly and says nothing year after year while the thing they refused to name quietly does its damage is not being wise. They are being afraid and calling it peace. The mantra is a legitimate corrective to that particular failure.

But the mantra applied without the filter of wisdom is not courage. It is speed with confidence. And speed with confidence has ended more relationships, damaged more communities, and done more unnecessary harm than silence ever did. Because silence at least leaves room for reconsideration. Words, once released, do their work regardless of the regret that follows them.

What Wisdom Has Been All Along

This series has covered a lot of ground. Leadership and followership. Marriage. Conflict. Communication. The gap between awareness and knowledge. The limits of mantras. But if the whole series were reduced to a single claim, it would be this.

Wisdom is not a set of techniques. It is not a communication style, a conflict management approach, or a leadership methodology. It is a quality of character, slowly formed over time, through honest self-examination, genuine encounter with Scripture, the pressure of real experience, and the willingness to be changed by what life brings rather than simply surviving it.

It grows slowly. It cannot be rushed. It does not respond to shortcuts. Every exam that was sat, every truth that was integrated through the friction of a real situation, every moment of choosing the right thing when the wrong thing was more immediately satisfying, these are the deposits from which wisdom is built. There are no other deposits.

James 1:5 remains the most generous invitation in the entire biblical wisdom tradition: if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given to him. The availability is unconditional. The giving is generous. The reproach is absent. But the asking requires something. It requires the honesty to acknowledge that you do not yet have what you are asking for. And that honesty, the willingness to stand before God and before your own life and say I do not yet know what I thought I knew, is itself the beginning of wisdom.

exists precisely in the space this series has been exploring. Not to give people more information about their lives but to help them understand them more deeply. To identify where the integration work still needs to happen. To name what has been circling without being addressed. To create the conditions in which truth can move from the place where it is known about to the place where it actually lives and governs.

Every person who has sat in an LTE session has come with knowledge. Information. Awareness of the truths that apply to their situation. What they have needed, and what the process is designed to provide, is not more of that. It is the honest examination that begins to close the gap between what they know and who they are.

That gap is where wisdom lives. And closing it, one honest examination at a time, one integrated truth at a time, one sat exam at a time, is the most significant work any person can do.

You do not need another mantra.

You need wisdom.

And wisdom, unlike a mantra, cannot be handed to you.

It has to be built in you.

One examined life at a time.

Blog Title: What Is Wisdom?
Blog Details: A serious exploration of the most needed and least taught quality of our time.
Blog Rich Title: What Is Wisdom?
Blog Rich Text:
Part One

A serious exploration of the most needed and least taught quality of our time.

We live in the most informed generation in human history. More data, more access, more credentials, more content than any previous era could have imagined. And yet, if you look honestly at the quality of decisions being made in our organisations, our governments, our homes, and our churches, a quiet and uncomfortable question begins to form.

Where is the wisdom?

Information is everywhere. Knowledge is accessible to almost anyone with a phone and a signal. Intelligence is celebrated and credentialed and rewarded. But wisdom, the capacity to take all of that and know what to actually do with it, is in remarkably short supply. And its absence is felt even by people who cannot name what is missing.

This is the first in a series of explorations on wisdom across a wide range of areas. Leadership, relationships, faith, suffering, speech, timing, money, and more. But before any of those conversations can mean anything, we have to start here. With the most fundamental question of all.

What is wisdom? What is it not? How do you recognise it when it is present? And why does it matter so deeply?

What Wisdom Actually Is

Wisdom is not intelligence. It is not the accumulation of knowledge, the possession of a high IQ, or the ability to think quickly under pressure. These things can exist entirely without wisdom, and in some cases they make the absence of wisdom more dangerous rather than less.

Wisdom is the capacity to see clearly, judge rightly, and act appropriately across the full complexity of real life. It integrates knowledge with experience, understanding with discernment, and principle with sensitivity to context. A wise person does not just know what is true. They know what to do with what is true, in this situation, at this moment, with these people, given what is actually at stake.

Robert Sternberg, one of the leading researchers on wisdom in contemporary psychology, defines it as the application of tacit knowledge toward a common good, balancing intrapersonal, interpersonal, and extrapersonal interests over the short and long term. In simpler language: wisdom knows how to navigate competing interests and realities in a way that serves something larger than itself.

Paul Baltes, another significant voice in wisdom research, described it as expert knowledge in the fundamental pragmatics of life. Not expertise in a technical field, but expertise in living itself. In navigating uncertainty, loss, relationship, purpose, and meaning with a quality of understanding that goes beyond information.

In the philosophical tradition, Aristotle distinguished between theoretical wisdom, the understanding of universal truths, and practical wisdom, which he called phronesis. Phronesis is the capacity to discern the right course of action in particular circumstances. It is wisdom that knows how to live, not just what to believe. Aristotle considered it the master virtue, the one that governs all the others.

Across these different frameworks a common thread emerges. Wisdom is integrative. It holds things together that lesser thinking pulls apart. Theory and practice. Principle and context. Individual interest and collective good. Short term and long term. Knowing and doing.

What Wisdom Is Not

Wisdom is not age. The assumption that wisdom comes automatically with years lived is one of the most persistent and damaging myths in circulation. Time can produce wisdom, but only if it has been accompanied by honest reflection, genuine learning from experience, and a willingness to be changed by what life brings. Without those things, age simply produces an older version of the same unexamined person.

Wisdom is not knowledge. You can know a great deal and still be unwise. In fact, the accumulation of knowledge without the corresponding development of judgment and character can produce a particularly dangerous kind of person. Someone with the tools to do significant harm and the intellectual confidence to justify it.

Wisdom is not cleverness. Cleverness finds shortcuts. Wisdom counts the cost of shortcuts. Cleverness wins arguments. Wisdom knows which arguments are worth having. Cleverness impresses rooms. Wisdom changes lives. They are not the same thing and in many settings they actively work against each other.

Wisdom is not caution. Some people mistake timidity for wisdom, the reluctance to act, the endless weighing of options, the avoidance of risk. But wisdom acts when action is required. It is not the absence of decisiveness. It is decisiveness rooted in genuine understanding rather than impulse or fear.

And wisdom is not spirituality. A person can be deeply spiritual and still be unwise. Sincere faith and poor judgment can coexist in the same person. This is not a criticism of faith. It is an honest observation that the life of faith requires wisdom as a companion, not a substitute for it.

What Scripture Says About Wisdom

The Bible takes wisdom with extraordinary seriousness. It is not a peripheral topic. It runs through the entire narrative of Scripture as one of the defining qualities of a life rightly lived.

Proverbs 9:10 establishes the foundation: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. This is not fear as terror but fear as reverent orientation. Wisdom, in the biblical framework, begins with correctly positioning yourself in relation to God. It starts with the acknowledgment that you are not the centre of all things, that there is a moral order in the universe that you did not create and cannot override, and that aligning yourself with that order is the beginning of seeing clearly.

Proverbs 8 gives wisdom a voice and lets her speak in the first person. She was present at creation. She calls out in the streets and the city gates. She is not hidden or esoteric. She is available, accessible, and actively seeking those who will receive her. The implication is that wisdom is not merely a human achievement. It is something given, something that comes from above and is received below.

James 1:5 is one of the most direct and generous promises in the New Testament: if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given to him. The availability of wisdom is not limited to the naturally gifted or the spiritually advanced. It is accessible to anyone willing to ask with genuine faith and genuine humility.

James 3:17 then describes what wisdom from above actually looks like when it arrives: pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. That is a character portrait. Wisdom, in Scripture, is not merely cognitive. It is moral. It shapes not just how you think but who you are and how you treat people.

And in 1 Corinthians 1:30, Paul identifies Christ himself as our wisdom. This is the deepest claim of all. True wisdom is not ultimately a set of principles or a cognitive capacity. It is a person. And the pursuit of wisdom, in the Christian life, is ultimately the pursuit of knowing Christ more fully.

How Do You Know Someone Is Wise?

Wisdom announces itself quietly. It rarely arrives with fanfare or self-promotion. In fact, one of the most reliable signs of wisdom is that the wise person is rarely the one insisting on their own wisdom.

A wise person holds complexity without collapsing it. They can sit with a difficult question without rushing to a premature answer. They can acknowledge that two things which seem to be in tension are both partially true. They resist the pull toward oversimplification even when oversimplification would be more comfortable or more popular.

A wise person reads situations accurately. They notice what others miss. They sense what is beneath the surface of a conversation or a decision. They are rarely surprised by consequences that others claim to have never seen coming, because they were watching for them.

A wise person knows the limits of their own knowledge. This is perhaps the most counterintuitive marker. The Dunning-Kruger effect in psychology describes how the least competent people tend to be the most confident, while genuine experts tend toward greater awareness of what they do not know. Wisdom operates the same way. The wiser a person becomes, the more clearly they see the edges of their own understanding.

A wise person takes the long view. They make decisions with an eye not just on the immediate outcome but on the downstream consequences. They are willing to accept short term discomfort for long term integrity. They are not easily seduced by what is expedient.

And a wise person is recognisable by the quality of their relationships. They tend to be trusted. Not necessarily liked by everyone, because wisdom sometimes requires saying what is difficult. But trusted. The people around them know that they will receive honest counsel, careful thought, and genuine regard for their wellbeing.

Why Wisdom Matters More Than Ever

We are living through a particular kind of crisis. Not primarily a crisis of information, we have more than enough of that. It is a crisis of judgment. Of knowing what to do with what we know. Of making decisions that account for complexity rather than reducing it. Of leading in ways that consider people rather than simply processing them.

The consequences of wisdom's absence are visible everywhere. In organisations that optimise for the short term and collapse in the long term. In leaders who are brilliant and destructive simultaneously. In relationships that break under the weight of being right rather than being wise. In faith communities that know their doctrine thoroughly and treat people carelessly.

Wisdom matters because life is genuinely complex, and complexity does not yield to cleverness alone. It yields to understanding. And understanding, the deep kind that integrates knowledge with experience and principle with humanity, is what wisdom produces.

It matters in your marriage, where knowing the right thing to say is far less important than knowing when to say it, how to say it, and when to say nothing at all. It matters in your leadership, where the gap between a good decision and a wise one can determine the health of everything you are responsible for. It matters in your faith, where the difference between knowing God and walking wisely with God is the difference between religion and life.

This is why wisdom sits at the heart of . Not as a subject to be studied but as a quality to be developed. LTE exists to help people move from scattered to purposeful, from information-rich to genuinely understanding, from knowing what they believe to knowing how to live it. That movement, from knowing to wisdom, is one of the most significant any person can make.

The series that follows this piece will explore what wisdom looks like in specific areas of life. Leadership, relationships, faith, suffering, speech, timing, and more. Each one building on the foundation laid here. Because you cannot recognise wisdom in action until you understand what wisdom actually is.

We do not need more information.

We need the wisdom to know what to do with what we already have.

That pursuit begins here.

Blog Rich Title: Who Let Them Lead?
Blog Rich Text:
A Reckoning With Leadership Failure Across Our Organisations, Nations, and Houses of Faith

You have sat in that meeting. You have watched that broadcast. You have listened to that sermon. And somewhere deep in your gut, a question has risen that you dare not say out loud.

How did this person get here?

No empathy. No foresight. No ability to look back and learn from what has already broken. No coherent vision for where things are going. And yet, there they are. At the top of the table. Signing off on decisions that will ripple through organisations, communities, nations, and generations. With a circle of advisors around them who nod in agreement before the sentence is even finished.

This is not a small problem. This is one of the defining crises of our time.

The System Selects the Wrong People

We like to tell ourselves that leadership is earned, that the best rise to the top through competence, character, and hard work. It is a comforting story. It is also largely a myth.

Most systems, corporate, political, religious, do not select for wisdom or empathy. They select for visibility, confidence, political savvy, and loyalty upward. The person who asks the hard questions gets labelled difficult. The one who slows things down to think carefully is seen as a bottleneck. The leader who admits uncertainty is perceived as weak. And so, quietly and systematically, the very qualities that make for genuinely good leadership get filtered out, while the ones that produce disaster get promoted.

This is not conspiracy. It is selection pressure. And it plays out the same way whether you are looking at a boardroom, a parliament, or a pulpit.

The Sycophant Problem

Bad leaders rarely arrive fully formed. Many start with good intentions. But power has a well-documented psychological effect. Research consistently shows that as people gain authority, their capacity for empathy measurably decreases. The brain literally begins to process other people differently. Add to this the comfort of privilege, the fear of losing what has been gained, and the slow migration of honest voices out of the inner circle, and you have a reliable recipe for collapse.

The sycophant circle is not merely annoying. It is catastrophic. When a leader surrounds themselves exclusively with people who affirm every instinct and validate every decision, they become completely insulated from reality. Feedback loops break. Warning signs go unheeded. And by the time consequences arrive, the damage is already done, while the leader remains genuinely convinced that everything was handled correctly.

Religious leadership carries a particular danger here. A bad CEO can be removed. A bad politician can lose an election. But a leader who anchors their authority in divine mandate, who says in effect that God has spoken through them, has placed themselves beyond accountability. And people of sincere faith, in their devotion, may surrender the very critical thinking that could protect them.

Selfishness at the Root

If you trace the dysfunction far enough, you almost always arrive at the same destination: selfishness. Not the crude, obvious kind, but the sophisticated, well-dressed variety that wraps itself in vision statements and strategic plans, in patriotic rhetoric, in spiritual language. The packaging looks like service. The engine underneath is self-preservation.

The tragedy is compounded by what we choose to celebrate. We complain about poor leaders in one breath and admire the ruthless deal-maker, the charismatic performer, the relentless climber in the next.

What we celebrate quietly, we eventually elect and appoint loudly.

If we want different leaders, we must first want different things.

Leadership Was Never Just a Position

Here is the truth that those in title-obsessed cultures do not want you to understand: leadership has never been fundamentally about position. It is about influence. And influence does not wait for permission.

The teacher who shapes how a child sees the world. The colleague who speaks a hard truth when everyone else is silent. The parent who models integrity when there is no audience. The community member who refuses to normalise what should be scandalous. These are acts of leadership, and they often matter more than anything happening in the offices and chambers above.

The rare leaders who leave lasting, positive legacies tend to share a quiet common thread. They did not need the room to agree with them. They could hold a conviction under pressure and also genuinely change their mind in the presence of truth. They stayed connected to real people outside their power structure, to honest relationships that told them what they needed to hear rather than what they wanted to hear, and to a moral anchor deeper than their own ambition.

What We Can Do From Where We Stand

The frustration with poor leadership is legitimate and important. But frustration alone changes nothing. The question is what we do with it within our own sphere of influence, however large or small that sphere may be.

We can refuse to become sycophants in environments that reward it. We can choose to be the person who tells the truth carefully but consistently, even when silence is more comfortable. We can model in our teams and families and communities the very kind of leadership we are missing above us, empathetic, accountable, visionary, and self-aware. We can be intentional about who we celebrate, who we follow, who we hand microphones and platforms and trust.

And perhaps most importantly, we can stay honest with ourselves. Because the most seductive lie in leadership discourse is the idea that we would be different, that we would handle power better, that the corrupting forces that shaped the people we criticise would somehow leave us untouched.

They probably would not.

This is one of the conversations that runs through the heart of . The question of leadership is not just about what happens in organisations and nations and pulpits. It begins inside each of us. In the choices we make when no one is watching. In the integrity we maintain when it costs something. In the kind of influence we choose to exercise in the rooms we already occupy. LTE exists to help people get serious about that interior work, because you cannot lead others well from an unexamined life.

The Question That Should Keep Us Up at Night

We have spent a great deal of energy diagnosing the problem, the empathy deficits, the echo chambers, the sycophant cultures, the systems that reward the wrong things. The diagnosis is important. But diagnosis without self-examination is just sophisticated complaining.

So here is the question worth sitting with. Not about them. About you.

In the spaces where you already have influence, your home, your team, your community, your relationships, are you leading the way you are demanding others lead? Or are you waiting for a position that may never come, while the opportunity to actually change something sits quietly in your hands right now?

Leadership is influence. Influence begins today.

You have been waiting for better leaders.

Perhaps they have been waiting for you.

Start where you are. Start today.

Blog Title: You Are Not Listening. You Are Waiting.
Blog Details: On the discipline of truly hearing another person, and why it is so much harder than it looks.
Blog Rich Title: You Are Not Listening. You Are Waiting.
Blog Rich Text:
On the discipline of truly hearing another person, and why it is so much harder than it looks.

Have you ever had something important to say and the person you were saying it to was simply not there?

Not physically absent. Sitting right in front of you. Eyes more or less in your direction. But somewhere behind those eyes, clearly somewhere else entirely. And you can feel it. You can feel the moment the connection drops. You can feel when your words are landing in an empty room.

You trail off. You lose the thread. You wrap up earlier than you meant to. And you leave the conversation carrying the thing you came to say, still unsaid, with the added weight of feeling like it did not matter enough to be properly received.

There are few things more quietly deflating than that experience. And there are few things more common.

Now here is the harder question. How often are you that person to someone else?

Five Signals You Are Not Truly Listening

Most people believe they are better listeners than they actually are. This is not arrogance. It is simply that poor listening is largely invisible to the person doing it. The signals are far more visible to the person on the other side of the conversation.

You interrupt mid-sentence. Not always aggressively. Sometimes with enthusiasm, sometimes finishing the thought helpfully. But the message received is the same: what I am about to say matters more than what you were still saying.

You finish people's thoughts for them. It feels like connection. It can actually be a subtle form of control, a way of steering the conversation toward where you expect it to go rather than where the other person was actually heading.

You redirect conversations back to yourself. Someone shares something difficult and within moments you have found a parallel experience of your own. It feels like empathy. It is often displacement. The other person's story becomes a doorway into yours.

You dismiss emotions as overreactions. You do not always say it directly. But the way you respond, the quick reframe, the rush to silver linings, the slightly impatient tone, communicates that the feeling is an obstacle rather than information worth receiving.

You respond before fully understanding context. You have already formed a view by the time the other person is halfway through. The rest of what they say is filtered through the conclusion you have already reached. This is where a great deal of leadership failure quietly begins.

Read that list again slowly. Most people will find themselves in at least two or three of those descriptions. Not because they are bad people. Because listening is genuinely hard, and nobody taught most of us how to do it well.

Listening Is Not Passive. It Is Disciplined Restraint.

The popular image of a good listener is someone who is quiet and patient, nodding attentively while another person speaks. That image is misleading because it makes listening look easy. It is not. Real listening is an active, demanding, even costly exercise.

It requires you to hold your own thoughts at bay while someone else is still forming theirs. It requires you to resist the impulse to fix, advise, reframe, or redirect before the other person has finished. It requires you to sit with silence without filling it. It requires you to receive something that may be uncomfortable without immediately making it more comfortable for yourself.

That is disciplined restraint. It is an act of will, repeated throughout every conversation, against the very natural pull of a mind that is always generating its next thought.

The Real Reason We Do Not Listen

Here is the part that rarely gets named. Most poor listening is not rudeness. It is anxiety.

The mind racing ahead to what to say next. The discomfort of silence that feels like emptiness. The need to be seen as capable, insightful, or helpful in the conversation. The fear of receiving something emotionally heavy and not knowing what to do with it. The habit of processing out loud rather than sitting quietly with what is being offered.

When you interrupt, you are often managing your own discomfort more than responding to the other person. When you redirect to your own experience, you are often reaching for familiar ground because sitting fully in someone else's experience feels exposed. When you dismiss emotions as overreactions, you are often protecting yourself from having to feel the weight of what is being shared.

Until the anxiety underneath poor listening is addressed, telling someone to listen better only scratches the surface. The behaviour is the signal. The root is somewhere deeper.

What Leaders Who Listen Actually Look Like

The strongest leaders are not those who speak first. They are those who understand first. This is not a soft observation. It is a strategic one. The leader who listens well makes fewer costly mistakes because they are working from fuller information. They build deeper trust because people feel genuinely received rather than processed. They spot problems earlier because they have not talked over the warning signs.

They are also harder to manipulate, because a person who listens carefully is not easily led by the loudest voice in the room. They have learned to distinguish between noise and signal, between what is being said and what is actually meant.

And in personal relationships, the leader who listens well is the spouse who makes their partner feel known rather than managed, the parent who makes their child feel safe enough to tell the truth, the friend who makes it possible to say the hard thing because the reception has always been generous.

Listening is one of the most significant acts of love available to any human being. And most of us are significantly underdeveloped in it.

Audit Your Conversations

One of the things that comes up repeatedly in sessions is the gap between how people intend to show up in their relationships and how they actually show up. Most people intend to listen. Very few have ever examined whether they actually do.

So here is a practical exercise worth taking seriously this week. Audit your conversations. Not in a self-critical or performance-oriented way, but with honest curiosity. Notice how many times you interrupt. Notice when you redirect toward yourself. Notice when you respond before the other person has finished. Notice when you feel the pull to fix or reframe rather than simply receive.

What you discover will tell you something important, not just about how you listen, but about the anxiety, the habits, and the patterns running underneath your conversations. And that is where the real work begins.

Because you cannot lead well, love well, or relate well from behind a wall of unexamined noise. Listening is not a communication skill. It is a character issue. And like every character issue, it responds to honest attention.

The strongest leaders are not those who speak first.

They are those who understand first.

Start there.

Blog Title: A Meditation on the Season Nobody Asks For and Everybody Needs
Blog Details: Nobody prays for a waiting season. But the seasons we resist most are often the ones doing the deepest work.
Blog Rich Title: A Meditation on the Season Nobody Asks For and Everybody Needs
Blog Rich Text:
Waiting

I am in a season of waiting as I write this. I say that plainly because I think it matters. This is not a reflection written from the comfortable distance of hindsight, with the outcome already known and the lesson already tidied up. I am in the middle of it. Fourteen years in, at the time of writing, with no resolution yet visible. And it is precisely from that middle place — where the silence is still loud and the answer is still outstanding — that I want to think through what waiting actually is, what it does to us, and what it is asking of us.

Most of us do not choose to wait. Waiting is chosen for us — by a process, by another person, by God, by circumstances that refuse to move at the pace we would prefer. And because it is imposed rather than elected, our first instinct is rarely acceptance. It is resistance. We check our emails again. We replay the application, the conversation, the decision, looking for something we might have missed. We oscillate between quiet confidence and quiet dread. We keep one ear permanently tilted toward the sound of an answer that has not yet come.

I know that place well. I suspect you do too.

What Waiting Actually Is

There is a temptation to treat waiting as empty time — a gap between the meaningful moments, a pause that has no content of its own. But I have come to believe that waiting is one of the most content-rich seasons a person can inhabit, precisely because it strips away the noise and forces an encounter with what is actually there.

When you are busy, you can avoid yourself almost indefinitely. The schedule fills. The output accumulates. The sense of forward motion creates the impression of progress. Waiting removes that covering. It puts you in a room with yourself and will not let you leave until you have sat with what is there. Your fears surface. Your assumptions become visible. Your theology gets tested in ways that comfortable seasons never quite manage.

Waiting is not empty time. It is a different kind of full — full of the things we usually move too fast to notice.

The Psalms are saturated with the language of waiting. David — a man of extraordinary action, a warrior and a king — wrote about waiting with a candour that is striking in its honesty. He did not perform patience. He described the ache of it, the question of it, the desperate reaching toward a God who seemed, from the inside of the experience, to be taking considerably longer than necessary.

"I waited patiently for the Lord; He turned to me and heard my cry. He lifted me out of the slimy pit, out of the mud and mire; He set my feet on a rock and gave me a firm place to stand." — Psalm 40:1-2

The phrase 'waited patiently' in the original Hebrew carries the sense of intense, straining expectation — the posture of someone leaning forward, watching, fully engaged. This is not the patience of indifference. It is the patience of someone who cares deeply about the outcome and has chosen, despite that care, to trust the one who holds it.

The Virtues Being Tested

Waiting puts specific things to the test. It is worth naming them honestly, because when you know what is being tested, the season becomes less bewildering.

Trust is the most obvious one. Every day that passes without an answer is a day in which you must choose, again, whether you believe that the God who knows about your situation is adequate to it. Trust is not a feeling. It is a repeated decision made in the absence of visible evidence. Waiting is where trust is built — precisely because it is where trust is tested most directly.

Identity is another. Waiting has a way of surfacing the question of who you are when you are not defined by your role, your output, or your next achievement. If your sense of self is heavily tied to what you produce or what you are recognised for, a season of waiting — where nothing is being produced publicly and recognition is on hold — will feel like an identity crisis. That is not a malfunction. It is an invitation to find a self that does not depend on circumstances to stay intact.

Contentment is a third. Paul wrote from a prison cell that he had learned to be content in all states — and the key word is learned. Contentment in waiting is an acquired capacity, developed through practice and through the slow, sometimes painful discovery that your life is not actually on hold. It is happening right now, in this season, with its own gifts and its own significance, whether or not the answer has arrived.

"I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content." — Philippians 4:11

How to Know It Is a Waiting Season

Sometimes the most disorienting part is not the waiting itself but the uncertainty about what kind of season you are actually in. Is this a waiting season — one in which the answer is coming and your role is to hold steady? Or is this a redirecting season — one in which the silence is itself a form of answer, pointing you elsewhere?

There is no formula for that discernment. But there are some markers worth paying attention to. A waiting season tends to carry a quality of settled unease — uncomfortable, yes, but not chaotic. There is something beneath the frustration that holds. A redirecting season often carries a growing sense of misalignment, a quiet but persistent signal that what you are waiting for may not be what you actually need. Both require attentiveness. Neither can be rushed into clarity.

What I have found is that the posture matters more than the answer to that question. A person who is genuinely open — to the answer coming, and to the possibility that something different is being prepared — tends to move through both kinds of seasons with more grace than someone who has decided in advance what the answer must be.

The Posture of Waiting

If I were to describe the posture that waiting asks of us, I would use three words: present, open, and rooted.

Present, because the great temptation of waiting is to live somewhere else — in the imagined future where the answer has arrived, or in the replayed past where you second-guess every decision that led to this moment. Both are ways of absenting yourself from the only place where life is actually happening, which is now. The waiting season has its own gifts, its own conversations, its own quiet work being done in you. You will miss them if you are not here.

Open, because certainty about the outcome is rarely available in a waiting season, and clutching too tightly to a particular answer closes you to the broader work God may be doing. Openness is not passivity. It is the active choice to hold your expectations loosely enough that something unexpected can still get through.

Rooted, because waiting has a way of testing what you are actually standing on. The storms of uncertainty reveal the foundations. A person rooted in the unchanging character of God — in His goodness, His faithfulness, His sufficiency — finds that the waiting, however long, does not ultimately move them. It shakes them, yes. It stretches them. But it does not uproot them.

"But those who wait on the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint." — Isaiah 40:31

The promise in Isaiah is not that waiting will be brief. It is that waiting, done in the right direction, produces a renewal that could not have been generated any other way. The eagle does not manufacture its own lift. It rises on currents that are already moving. Waiting, at its best, is the posture of a person who has learned to trust the current — even when it is not yet visible.

I am still in mine. Fourteen years and counting. And I am learning, slowly, that this season is not a gap in my story. It is part of it. Perhaps one of the more important parts.

Whatever you are waiting for — I hope you find that too.

Blog Rich Title: The Conversation We Keep Avoiding
Blog Rich Text:
Why intimacy in marriage is not a private matter — it is a life transformation issue

────────────────────────

Debo Owoseni

Convener,

I am going to say something that many platforms will not. Probably because it's an uncomfortable truth, and I have learned, in life and in the work of transformation, that the things which make us most uncomfortable are usually the things we most need to face.

Intimacy in marriage is not a bedroom issue. It is a life issue. It sits at the root of more marital breakdown, emotional instability, personal stagnation, and productivity than most couples, counsellors, therapist and church leaders are willing to admit. We dress the symptoms. We treat the surface. We have long, careful conversations about communication styles and love languages and conflict resolution — and we never quite get to the thing that is actually broken underneath all of it.

I am speaking from experience. Not from a theory or a research paper. I have been in the place I am describing, and I am writing this because I know what it costs to stay there, and I know what becomes possible when you are finally honest enough to address it.

The things that make us most uncomfortable are usually the things we most need to face.

The Misdiagnosis That Is Destroying Marriages

A couple comes for counselling. The presenting issues are familiar: poor communication, emotional distance, frequent arguments, one partner withdrawn and the other frustrated. The counsellor works through the standard frameworks. There is progress, briefly. Then the same patterns return.

What no one asked — what no one felt comfortable asking — is what is happening in the physical and emotional intimacy of that marriage. Because the answer, in a significant number of cases, would explain almost everything else on the list.

Unmet intimacy needs do not simply disappear. They migrate. They surface as irritability that seems disproportionate to its trigger. They show up as emotional unavailability, as resentment that the person carrying it cannot quite explain, as a creeping sense that something is fundamentally wrong with the relationship even when nothing obvious has happened. The person who is consistently neglected or rejected in this area does not always have the language to name it. They just know they feel alone in a house full of people. They just know they have stopped reaching out. They just know something essential has quietly died.

Unmet intimacy needs do not disappear. They migrate — into resentment, withdrawal, anger and a loneliness that has no name.

We are doing marriages a disservice by treating these symptoms while refusing to examine the root. Honest diagnosis is not unkind. Continued misdiagnosis is.

The One Thing That Cannot Be Outsourced

Think carefully about what can be shared or delegated in a marriage. Cooking, finances, childcare, emotional support, social obligations, in a crisis, or even in a season of strain, all of these can draw from other sources. A friend can provide companionship. A parent can step in with the children. A colleague can offer professional encouragement.

But conjugal intimacy belongs exclusively within the marriage covenant. It cannot be outsourced. It cannot be substituted. It is the one dimension of a married person's life that their spouse holds the exclusive key to. Which means that when it is withheld, neglected, or treated as optional, the wound it creates has nowhere else to go. There is no alternative source. There is no workaround. There is only the daily reality of a legitimate need going unmet inside the one relationship that was designed to meet it.

Everything in a marriage can, in a crisis, be drawn from somewhere else. Conjugal intimacy cannot. It belongs exclusively to the covenant.

This is not merely a physical observation. Scripture treats the marriage union with a seriousness that our casualness about intimacy frankly contradicts. Paul, writing to the Corinthians, is remarkably direct: a husband and wife's bodies belong to each other. The withholding of intimacy, except by mutual consent and for a defined season, is treated as a deprivation with real spiritual consequences. This is not a peripheral instruction. It sits at the heart of the covenant.

So when I ask the question you may have felt coming: if you knew you were not willing or ready to address the factors that would prevent you from meeting your spouse's intimacy needs, why did you marry? It is not a cruel question. It is an honest one. And honest questions are the beginning of real change.

The Mind Is the Real Sex Organ

Here is where the conversation opens up in a way that should actually be encouraging.

Sexuality is not primarily located in the body. It is located in the mind. The body follows where the mind leads. This is why you can be in the presence of a naked stranger and feel nothing, while your spouse removes a jacket and something stirs in you. The physical is the same. The mind is what is different. Context, meaning, relationship, safety, desire — these are all processed in the mind. The body simply responds.

This matters enormously for couples navigating difficulty in this area. Because it means the solution is rarely physical. It means that conversations, attitudes, habits of thought, patterns of relating, and the willingness to be emotionally present are doing far more work than most people realise. It means that fixing intimacy in a marriage is, in most cases, not as complicated as people make it. The body will follow when the mind is genuinely engaged.

The mind is the most versatile and powerful sexual organ. Fix what is happening there, and the body tends to follow.

What makes it feel complicated is not the complexity of the problem. It is the unwillingness of one or both parties to honestly face the factors that are creating the block. Fear. Past wounds. Unspoken resentment. Shame. A quietly held belief that their own needs and comfort matter more than the covenant they made. These are mind issues, not body issues. And mind issues can be addressed — through honest conversation, through professional support where needed, through the decision, made daily, to prioritise the person you married.

Helplessness Is a Choice

I want to say this as plainly as I can, because I think it needs to be said.

There is a difference between struggling and refusing. There is a difference between finding something genuinely difficult and deciding, consciously or unconsciously, that your discomfort is more important than your spouse's wholeness. Many people who present as helpless in this area are not, in truth, helpless. They are unwilling. And unwillingness dressed as helplessness is one of the more dishonest postures a person can take inside a marriage.

If you are the party creating the deficit in your marriage's intimacy life, the people affected by your choice extend further than you may have considered. Your spouse is affected. Your children, who absorb the emotional temperature of the home they grow up in, are affected. The productivity, the vision, the sense of purpose and possibility that your spouse carries into the world every day — all of that is shaped, more than anyone likes to admit, by what is or is not happening in the intimacy of your home.

You may not be doing this for your own sake. But do it for the sake of who your spouse is trying to become, and the world they are trying to build.

This is a life transformation issue. It always has been. The person who is consistently depleted at this level does not show up fully in their work, their parenting, their purpose, or their faith. You cannot compartmentalise a wound this central. It bleeds into everything.

Five Honest Steps Toward Healing

These are not quick fixes. They are the beginning of an honest journey that many couples have taken and found to be genuinely transformative.

1.

Name the Reality in the Room

Nothing changes until someone is willing to say, clearly and without blame, that something is broken and needs attention. This conversation is hard. It is also necessary. Choose a calm moment, not a heated one, and begin with what you are experiencing rather than what your spouse is doing wrong. The goal of the first conversation is not resolution. It is honesty. Opening the door is enough to start with.

Reflect: Have we ever actually named this directly, or have we only ever argued around it?

2.

Identify the Real Blockage

In most cases, the intimacy deficit is a symptom of something else — unresolved conflict, unspoken resentment, fear, past trauma, shame, or a deeply held belief about one's own body or worth. Do the honest work of identifying what is actually creating the withdrawal or the resistance. This may require individual reflection, journalling, prayer, or professional support. But the blockage must be named before it can be addressed.

Reflect: What is the real reason intimacy has become difficult, and have I been honest about that with myself?

3.

Build Routine and Intentionality

Intimacy does not sustain itself. It requires deliberate investment, especially in seasons of busyness, stress, or relational strain. Couples who thrive in this area are almost always couples who have made intentional decisions about it — creating time, reducing the conditions that kill desire, and treating connection as a priority rather than an afterthought. Romance is not a feeling that either exists or does not. It is a discipline that produces feelings over time.

Reflect: What practical changes would make genuine connection more possible in our home right now?

4.

Seek Competent Support Without Shame

Sex therapy, marital counselling, and pastoral support exist because these issues are real, common, and addressable. The shame that keeps people from seeking help is costing them years of unnecessary pain. A competent therapist working in this area can, in a relatively short time, help couples identify the specific patterns and beliefs that are creating difficulty and provide practical tools for change. Seeking help is not weakness. Continuing to suffer in silence when help is available is simply a waste.

Reflect: What has stopped us from seeking support, and is that reason genuinely worth what it is costing us?

5.

Choose Your Spouse Daily

Ultimately, the intimacy of a marriage is sustained by a series of daily, unglamorous decisions to prioritise the person you married. To stay curious about them. To remain emotionally present. To resist the drift toward parallel lives that busyness and familiarity can produce. The couples who sustain genuine intimacy across decades are not lucky. They are intentional. They decided that their spouse's wholeness mattered enough to keep choosing, even when choosing required something from them.

Reflect: In the small, daily decisions of this week, am I choosing my spouse or choosing my comfort?

A Final Word

is committed to honest conversations about the things that actually shape a life. And few things shape a life more quietly, more persistently, and more profoundly than the quality of intimacy in a marriage.

This is not a topic for the faint-hearted. But transformation never is. It requires the willingness to look at what is real, name what is broken, and make the sustained, courageous decision to do the work.

Your spouse deserves that. Your children deserve it. And if you are honest, so do you.

────────────────────────

So here is the question to sit with:

If the intimacy of your marriage were a measure of how seriously you take your covenant, what would it be telling you right now?

────────────────────────

Blog Title: What Nobody Tells You About Getting Close to a Leader
Blog Details: Proximity to leadership is a privilege that comes with an unwritten cost. What you gain in access, you may lose in something else entirely.
Blog Rich Title: What Nobody Tells You About Getting Close to a Leader
Blog Rich Text:
A conversation for those who are already close enough to see clearly, and are still trying to figure out what to do with what they see.

A word before we begin. This article will not make sense to everyone. Those who have only ever admired leaders from a comfortable distance may find it unsettling. Those whose entire identity is wrapped up in celebrating a leader may find it threatening. And those who have never been close enough to see past the pulpit or platform may find it hard to believe.

This is written for the person who is already inside. Who has served closely, seen clearly, and is quietly trying to make sense of the terrain they find themselves in.

A final word in this opening. If you are a leader reading this, you may find parts of it uncomfortable. That is not the intention and this is not a veiled critique or an attempt to call you out. If anything, this is written with deep respect for the weight of what you carry. But honest conversation about the terrain of leadership proximity is largely absent from leadership training, ministry schools, and the platforms where leaders are developed. That absence is not serving anyone well. Not the leaders. Not the people who serve alongside them. And not the generation coming behind who will one day find themselves in the same delicate space with no map and no language for what they are experiencing.

From a distance, top leaders, including church leaders, look extraordinary. Pastors, bishops, evangelists, apostles. They carry an undeniable weight. There is something real in the room when they walk in. The anointing is not imagination. The calling is not performance. The influence is genuine and the fruit, in many cases, is significant.

But then you get close.

And close is a completely different country.

Up close you begin to notice things that the crowd never sees. You notice that care does not always appear to flow equally, that some people in the inner circle appears favoured and others quietly overlooked. You notice that subjectivity appears to creep into decisions that are presented as spiritual. You notice that those who give generously may tend to receive more attention, while those who serve faithfully in the background are rarely checked on. You notice that feedback is sparse, sometimes completely absent, and that the silence can feel heavier than any word of correction ever could.

You notice moments of anger that pass quickly but leave a mark. You notice that the person who carries so much for so many does not always have the capacity to carry the people closest to them. And you notice, with a quiet ache, that the ones who give the most to the leader are sometimes the ones least looked after by the leader.

And then there are the personal struggles, because leaders are human, fully and completely human, and the weight of what they carry does not make them immune to the things that unsettle every other person. It sometimes makes those things worse.

None of this cancels the calling. But it does complicate everything.

The Delicate Space Nobody Prepares You For

There is a tension that comes with proximity to leadership that very few people name honestly. On one side, you do not want to get so familiar that you lose your sense of honour, because with familiarity comes a contempt that will cost you. The well of anointing and influence that a leader carries is real, and access to it is a gift that should not be squandered through carelessness or overfamiliarity.

On the other side, you cannot be so distant or so captured by the image of the leader that you become a praise singer, a sycophant who validates everything and questions nothing. That posture does not serve the leader, does not serve the people around them, and certainly does not serve your own integrity.

Right in the middle of that tension is where most people who work closely with church leaders actually live. And it is a difficult, often lonely, rarely discussed place to be.

What You Do With What You See

Here is the part that most people do not realise until they are already in it: what you do with what you see reveals far more about your own character than it reveals anything new about the leader.

When you see the flaw, you have choices. You can expose it, and in doing so position yourself as the one who is more righteous, more discerning, more worthy. You can excuse it, and in doing so compromise your own integrity and enable something that may eventually harm many people. You can become cynical, quietly withdrawing your heart while maintaining the appearance of loyalty. Or you can cover it wisely, which is the rarest and most costly of all the options.

Covering wisely is not the same as covering up. It does not mean pretending what you see is not there. It means choosing not to make someone else's unresolved humanity your primary conversation. It means praying for what you cannot speak about. It means maintaining honour for the office even when the person in the office disappoints you. And it means being honest with yourself about what you can carry and what you cannot compromise.

The Doctrine of Leadership

This is where what I call the doctrine of leadership becomes essential. Doctrine in this sense is not theology on a page. It is a governing principle, a load-bearing conviction that holds your behaviour in place when your feelings are pulling in a completely different direction.

There are things you do not do because you feel like doing them. There are things you do not say because they are true. There are positions you hold, services you render, and honours you extend not because the person in front of you has earned them in that moment, but because the doctrine, the principle of how kingdom leadership works, requires it of you.

This is not blind obedience. It is not the suspension of discernment. It is the decision to operate from a standard higher than your feelings, higher than your assessment of the moment, and higher than the disappointment of what you have seen. It is maturity in its most demanding form.

Why Proximity Is Still Worth It

Despite everything, proximity to leadership remains one of the most accelerating environments for personal growth available to a believer. Not because leaders are perfect. Precisely because they are not.

Getting close grows you in ways that comfortable distance never will. It tests your loyalty in real time. It develops your capacity to honour something larger than your personal feelings. It gives you access to wisdom, opportunity, and influence that you could not build alone. And the seeds you plant in that season, faithfulness when it is inconvenient, service when it is unseen, integrity when no one is checking, those seeds have a harvest that comes in its own time.

There have been seasons in my own journey where I moved up the leadership ladder, began to see things clearly, and made the choice to withdraw. At the time it felt like wisdom. And sometimes it was. But I have also come to understand that some of those withdrawals were tests I was meant to pass, not situations I was meant to exit. The discomfort of what I saw was not a signal to leave. It was an invitation to go deeper in my own character.

The flaws of a leader, when handled with wisdom and a clean heart, can make you. They can develop in you the very qualities that will be required when it is your turn to lead. The alternative, allowing what you see to make you bitter, cynical, or superior, can mar you in ways that take years to undo.

The Test You Did Not Know You Were Taking

Here is what I have come to believe after walking this terrain more than once: the proximity to a flawed leader is rarely an accident. It is often a carefully designed test for your calling.

God does not place you close to a difficult leader to torture you. He places you there to find out, and to show you, what you are made of. Whether you can honour without idolising. Whether you can see without judging. Whether you can serve without needing to be seen. Whether you can cover without losing yourself. Whether you can stay when everything in you wants to go.

Passing that test does not mean staying forever in a situation that is genuinely harmful. There are seasons that end and transitions that are necessary. But passing it does mean that when you leave, if you leave, you leave with your integrity intact, without bitterness, without a story you are telling anyone who will listen, and without the kind of unresolved anger that follows you into the next season.

Your calling needs roots. And roots do not grow in comfortable soil. They grow under pressure, in the dark, and often in terrain that nobody else can see.

The terrain of leadership proximity is difficult, delicate, and largely unseen.

But for those who navigate it with wisdom, honour, and a clean heart, they make even greater leaders!

The terrain of leadership proximity is one of the most powerful leadership classrooms God has ever designed.

You Cannot Run From Marriage

Why marriage is everybody's business, whether you want it to be or not

Debo Owoseni | Transformation Architect

You may think this article is not for you. You are not married. Or you tried it and it cost you too much. Or marriage simply sits outside the season you are in right now.

Stay with this anyway. Because what follows is going to reframe something you thought you already understood.

Marriage Is Not a Private Matter

In the United States alone, a marriage ends every 42 seconds. Between 40 and 50 percent of first marriages collapse. Second marriages fail at a rate of nearly 60 percent. Third marriages at 73 percent. And those are just the ones that officially end. The ones that stay together but have quietly died on the inside are a different and much larger number.

These are American figures because America captures data. The reality in other parts of the world is likely worse, not better. The numbers are just harder to see.

But here is what those statistics do not capture. Every marriage that struggles, breaks, or fails does not just affect the two people inside it. It produces children, shapes colleagues, forms leaders, and influences communities. The damage or the health of a marriage radiates outward in ways that most people never trace back to their source.

Marriage is not a private institution. It is a public force. What happens inside one does not stay inside one.

The People Around You Came From Somewhere

Think about the people who have the most influence over your daily life right now.

Your boss, the one whose mood sets the tone of your entire workplace, came from a home. The friend who has your child's ear right now came from a home. The politician whose decisions shape the policies you live under came from a home. Your colleagues, your neighbours, the person sitting across from you in a relationship came from homes. Every single one of them was formed inside a family that was built around a marriage. By what that marriage produced. Or by what it failed to produce.

The instability you sometimes feel in leadership around you. The emotional unavailability in people close to you. The patterns that show up in your relationships that you cannot fully explain. Many of these trace back to marriages. Specifically, to what was modelled, what was broken, and what was never taught inside the homes that produced the people now surrounding you.

You are already living with the consequences of other people's marriages. The question is whether you are aware of it.

Even Jesus. Even Paul.

Some people arrive at this conversation with a ready objection. Jesus was not married. Paul was not married. Two of the most significant figures in Christian history chose singleness. So surely marriage is optional, even for the most committed believer.

True. And beside the point.

Jesus was raised in a home. Mary and Joseph's home. A marriage shaped the earthly environment of the Son of God. The stability, the faithfulness, and the obedience of that union provided the context in which Jesus grew in wisdom and stature before God and man.

Paul, who chose not to marry, wrote more extensively about marriage than almost any other subject across his letters. He addressed husbands and wives, described the relationship between Christ and the church through the lens of marriage, and gave detailed instruction on how marriage should function. A man who never married spent a significant portion of his ministry speaking into one.

Even the two most celebrated unmarried figures in Scripture could not avoid the influence and the weight of marriage. Neither can you.

The Ripple Goes Further Than You Think

When a marriage is healthy, it produces secure people. People who know how to attach, how to trust, how to navigate conflict, how to commit. Those people go into workplaces, governments, schools, and communities and they bring that security with them. It shows up in how they lead, how they parent, how they relate.

When a marriage is broken or toxic or absent, it produces a different kind of person. Not a lesser person. But a person carrying wounds that will show up somewhere. In their parenting. In their leadership. In their friendships. In their marriages. The ripple does not stop at the front door of the home it came from.

This is why the state of marriage is not just a personal or religious concern. It is a social one. A cultural one. A generational one. Every generation is downstream of the marriages that came before it.

Going Back to the Design

If the problem is this deep and this wide, the answer has to go back just as far. Patching individual marriages with communication tips and date night schedules is not enough. We need to go back to the original design. To understand what marriage was built to be, what it was built to produce, and how it was meant to function from the beginning.

That is the purpose of Back to Basics: Marriage 101. This is not a series for people in crisis, though it will help them. It is not only for the newly married, though they will gain the most from starting here. It is for anyone who wants to understand marriage at its foundations. Because understanding the design is the only way to make sense of what goes wrong when the design is ignored.

Irrespective of your beliefs about marriage. Irrespective of your marital status. As long as you live in this world and among other people, you are living inside the influence of marriage. That makes this conversation relevant to every one of us.

You cannot run from marriage. So let us learn to understand it, build it, and protect it the way God always intended.

This Is Your Invitation

Whether you are in a marriage right now, preparing to enter one, healing from one, or simply trying to understand the ones shaping the world around you, this series was built for you.

The conversation starts soon. And it is one you cannot afford to miss.
